decisions.decision: Use the postprocessing library for screen effects instead of writing every pass by hand
decisions.why: It merges effects into one or two full-screen passes, which is what keeps bloom, god rays and grading affordable on integrated graphics.

decisions.decision: All surfaces are made by one MaterialKit that shares one set of shader inputs
decisions.why: The color sweep, fog and theme then work on every object in every scene without scene authors thinking about it, and a sweep costs nothing per material.

decisions.decision: Effects are animated on the graphics card from ring buffers
decisions.why: Spawning an effect writes a few numbers; nothing is allocated while playing, which the performance rules require.

decisions.decision: The benchmark runs on medium and judges steadiness, not just average speed
decisions.why: A browser never draws faster than the screen, so high is only chosen when 95 percent of frames are on time.

decisions.decision: The draw-call budget is enforced on low and medium only
decisions.why: ARCHITECTURE sets the budget for medium; high and ultra spend extra draw calls on cascaded shadows by design (about 260 in the range).

decisions.decision: On the night-ink theme the forgotten-world grey is lifted to a moonlit level
decisions.why: The dark fade token is nearly black; when I looked at the range in the dark theme the whole ground was pure black. It is now dim but readable.

decisions.decision: The test range is reached by address (#/range) and is not in the menus
decisions.why: It is a tool for building scenes, not part of the game.

decisions.decision: Audio and HUD are silent stand-ins in SceneContext for now
decisions.why: They are built in T09 and T10; scenes written today will not need changing when they arrive.

decisions.decision: With reduce motion on, shake, push-in, flash, chromatic pulse and hit-stop are switched off completely
decisions.why: Those are exactly the effects that bother motion-sensitive players; color sweeps and particles stay.

decisions.decision: Applied the two new owner rules (merged into main while this task was being built) inside this task
decisions.why: They are binding for every task: the range had one figure in a head scarf that could be read as a woman, and its words came from the whole library instead of the learned letters.

decisions.decision: Before enough letters are learned to spell real words, the range shows short drills made of the learned letters
decisions.why: A new player knows only two keys; nothing unlearned may ever be asked, so drills are the only honest text.

manual_steps.title: Check the frame rate on a real computer
manual_steps.details: The cloud build machine has no graphics card, so real speed could not be measured there. On your own computer open the live link, add #/range to the end of the address, click Medium under Quality and read the first line of the small box in the corner: it should say about 60 and not be red. Needs the live link from the T01 step (Import the repo into Vercel).
manual_steps.browser_prompt: Open the live Otiyot website in my browser (the Vercel address of the project shlomyeisenberg-lang/Otiyot; if you do not know it, open https://vercel.com/dashboard, open the project named otiyot and use its production address; if asked to sign in, stop and hand control back to me). Steps: 1) Add #/range to the end of the address and press Enter. 2) If the welcome steps appear, type the name Test, press Enter, then click Next twice, then go to the #/range address again. 3) Wait about 5 seconds until the 3D scene appears. 4) In the Quality group click Medium. 5) Wait 5 seconds, then read the small box in the top corner: frames per second, frame time, draw calls, triangles. 6) Press the number keys 1 to 9 one at a time and read frames per second again. 7) Click High and read the numbers once more. Stop and hand control back to me for sign-in, passwords, 2FA, CAPTCHAs, payment and creating an account; never type a secret yourself. When done, report the numbers you read for Medium and High, whether any number was shown in red, and what computer and browser this is.

manual_steps.details: The cloud machine has no graphics card, so the fight was checked at about 2 frames per second. On your own computer open the live link, add #/range to the end of the address, click Calm and then Easy under Wave fight, and type the words on the Blots' shields. Then try Steady and Swift. manual_steps.browser_prompt: Open the live Otiyot website in my browser (the Vercel address of the project shlomyeisenberg-lang/Otiyot; if you do not know it, open https://vercel.com/dashboard, open the project named otiyot and use its production address; if asked to sign in, stop and hand control back to me). Stop and hand control back to me for sign-in, passwords, 2FA, CAPTCHAs, payment and creating an account; never type a secret yourself. When done, report the rank, the numbers on the results card, the frames per second, and anything that looked broken.

decisions.decision: The Great Blot is its own region (blot, Act One) that opens once the Cliffs are restored, fought in the Silent Arena shell; the later Arena region (T26) stays as it was.
decisions.why: The roadmap makes the first boss the end of the Phase 1 slice (title, hub, two scenes, boss), while the Arena region opens only at course level 6 and T26 adds three more bosses there. decisions.decision: "Unlocks Phase 2 scenes" is a story gate: Act Two and Three regions keep their course need and also wait for the Great Blot (after: blot); the map says "First defeat the Great Blot".
decisions.why: The story should not skip its first boss, but the course still decides when each scene opens. A player who beats the Blot loses nothing; the Blot is beatable on Calm by anyone who reached it.

decisions.decision: Health is the share of the fight text still unwritten, and attacks never fail the player (they drop the streak); only the Sofer’s Trial fails, on the first error.
decisions.why: Guarantees the fight is winnable on every difficulty with no soft-lock, matches GAME_DESIGN (only hardcore modes fail), and keeps the pressure honest: stalling costs streak, not progress.

decisions.decision: Attack timing per difficulty is a gentle typing pace (Steady 9, Swift 15, Fierce 22, Trial 16 WPM plus a grace of 2.6 to 3.6 s per group); on Calm the attack creeps in and waits.
decisions.why: An attack should land only when the player stops or slows a lot, never because a beginner is a beginner.

decisions.decision: The twist in Phase IV is an order twist: the words swallowed in Phase I come back last first, while the world turns inside out (ink sky, pale Blot, a camera roll). No layout switch.
decisions.why: A Hebrew to English switch would ask for keys the player has not learned on the other layout, which the content rules forbid; the mirror keeps it learned-letters-only and still feels sudden.

decisions.decision: Checkpoints are kept on Calm, Steady and Swift as story flags (boss:blot:2..4) and resume automatically, with a card saying so; "Start the fight again" and a victory forget them.
decisions.why: The roadmap asks for checkpoints on lower difficulties; flags fit the save without a schema change or migration.

decisions.decision: The fight is one typing run per phase; the streak is carried between phases, and the results merge the per-phase numbers (mergeMetrics).
decisions.why: The typing driver ends a run at its text; one run per phase lets the transition pause the quill cleanly while the result still counts the whole fight.

R15.summary: Opus reviewed Sonnet's Cliffs of Ein Gedi (T15) and played it in English and Hebrew at desktop and phone width. The scene is solid and good-looking; one real gameplay flaw was fixed: in English the stones climbed to the top and then stayed flat, so 'reach up' stopped meaning anything.

tests/unit/cliffs.test.ts: new tests that a fluent player gets both reaches, at most one flat 'reach' per run, a balanced up/down count, and that reachCost scores bad steps as poor fits (English and Hebrew, all levels, 12 seeds).

decisions.decision: Steadiness is measured against the player's own pace (a slow moving average of the gaps between keys), not a fixed tempo.
decisions.why: The task asks to reward consistency, not speed; a beginner typing slowly but evenly gets the same current as a fast typist, and nobody is pushed to rush.

decisions.decision: Gaps longer than 2.2 seconds count as a rest and are not judged.
decisions.why: A breath between words or a moment to read should never be punished; only the rhythm inside the typing counts.

decisions.decision: Nothing fails or blocks: an uneven or rushed page still rises (slowly, not gold), and bursts only cloud the water.
decisions.why: Same rule as every scene: no timers, no soft-locks, the run always finishes; the reward for steadiness is gold pages, a clear hall and the results card.

decisions.why: A unit test requires every theme to have its own melody instrument; the cello was the only one left and suits a deep, slow underwater hall.
